claims.text: Six systems were surveyed for cross-file invariant cataloging patterns: Terraform's precondition/postcondition lifecycle blocks, dbt's properties.yml data tests with ref, OpenAPI's components + $ref, JSON Schema's $defs + $ref, ArchUnit's ArchRule/ArchModule plus the shareable rules-library pattern, and Bazel's package_group for cross-package visibility invariants.
claims.notes: Scope-setting claim listing the six surveyed systems.

claims.text: Across all six surveyed systems, the authoring surface is denormalized (each artifact carries its own declarations), but reusable rule bodies and identifiers are factored into a centralized catalog and referenced.
claims.notes: Load-bearing synthesis claim: hybrid model consensus across surveyed systems.

claims.text: None of the surveyed systems adopt a fully centralized authoring model in which a single file owns all cross-file invariants.
claims.notes: Negative finding: pure-centralized authoring model is not exemplified by any surveyed system.

claims.text: Terraform's precondition and postcondition blocks live inside each resource, data, or output block's lifecycle block.
In Terraform, the precondition/postcondition condition expression can reference any other object in the same configuration scope, but there is no global invariant catalog file.
Terraform documentation states: 'You can refer to any other object in the same configuration scope unless the reference creates a cyclic dependency.'
claims.notes: Verbatim quote from HashiCorp lifecycle/validate docs.

claims.text: Terraform's precondition/postcondition expressions are authored where the resource is declared, and Terraform evaluates the conditions in dependency order at plan/apply time.

Terraform supports check blocks (v1.5.0+) which can be authored as standalone blocks rather than inside a resource — closer to a centralized assertion but still authored at top level alongside resources, not in a separate catalog file.
claims.notes: Caveat about Terraform check blocks.

claims.text: Terraform module input-variable validation blocks are per-variable, not centralized.

HashiCorp explicitly tells authors that the choice between precondition and postcondition is about whose responsibility the invariant represents — the consumer's assumption versus the producer's guarantee — and recommends placing each invariant near the block whose author should maintain it.
claims.notes: Encodes the 'invariant lives with the artifact whose author maintains it' locality discipline.

claims.text: Terraform's precondition-vs-postcondition guidance is a locality argument: invariants live with the artifact whose author is best-placed to keep them current.

dbt allows model invariants (data tests, relationships referential-integrity tests, descriptions) to be declared in properties.yml files (formerly schema.yml) located either per-model, per-directory, or as a single project-wide file.
The dbt official FAQ explicitly leaves the choice of property-file granularity (per-model, per-directory, or project-wide) to the team.
dbt's relationships test is the cross-file invariant: it uses ref() to assert that every value in a child column has a corresponding parent row.
dbt official docs include the quote: 'Some folks find it useful to have one file per model... Some find it useful to have one per directory.'
claims.notes: Verbatim quote from dbt FAQ.

claims.text: dbt has explicitly renamed the file from schema.yml to properties.yml and updated its terminology, encouraging authors to think of these as resource-property files (denormalized by default) rather than a centralized 'schema' catalog.
Practitioner guides converge on folder-level YAML (_[directory]__models.yml) as the best default for dbt because one-file-per-model creates churn and one-monolithic-file harms discoverability.
claims.notes: Medium confidence: derived from Semantic Stack practitioner guide, not official dbt-labs.

claims.text: The Semantic Stack guide states: 'A single monolithic YAML file centralizes config but makes specific tests, descriptions, and source definitions hard to find.'
claims.notes: Verbatim quote from Semantic Stack practitioner guide; surfaces the locality-vs-discoverability trade-off.

claims.text: OpenAPI consolidates reusable schemas, parameters, responses, request bodies, security schemes, and other reusable objects into #/components/<type>/<name>.
The OpenAPI spec permits $ref anywhere a reference is valid, and the OpenAPI Initiative's learn.openapis.org referencing guide states reusable definitions belong in components.
Engineering guides treat inlining repeated schemas in OpenAPI as a documented anti-pattern.
The OpenAPI Components Object 'holds a set of reusable objects for different aspects of the OAS.'
claims.notes: Verbatim quote from OpenAPI Specification v3.1.2.

claims.text: OpenAPI 3.1 introduced sibling-keyword support for $ref (siblings like description are honored), which slightly narrows the spec gap between centralized and inline forms.

Bump.sh's advanced $ref guide names the central-vs-inline trade-off directly: splitting components reduces merge conflicts and DRY violations but 'becomes harder to follow API changes' because a single schema edit affects many endpoints.
claims.notes: Vendor engineering blog; medium confidence per source constraints.

claims.text: Bump.sh proposes that the remedy for the OpenAPI change-tracking opacity introduced by centralization is automated breaking-change detection on PRs, not abandoning centralization.
claims.notes: Load-bearing consensus-mitigation claim: tooling, not retreat.

claims.text: Bump.sh states: 'Changing a schema in one document can effect how multiple different endpoints work.'
claims.notes: Verbatim quote from Bump.sh blog.

claims.text: JSON Schema's $defs keyword (since draft 2019-09; previously definitions) 'gives us a standardized place to keep subschemas intended for reuse in the current schema document.'
claims.notes: Verbatim quote from official JSON Schema docs.

claims.text: JSON Schema cross-document $ref works but the official guide recommends limiting $ref to either an external schema or an internal $defs-defined subschema, and recommends bundling external resources into $defs for distribution.
JSON Schema 'Compound Schema Documents' (bundles) are an implementation concern — the authoring surface remains per-file with selective central reuse.

JSON Schema cautions implementers to disable dynamic remote $ref retrieval by default for security and resource-exhaustion reasons, which structurally biases practice toward in-document $defs over true cross-file central catalogs.
ArchUnit's ArchRules are declared as static fields in JUnit test classes; the user guide and engineering write-ups show rules written in the repository that owns the code under test.

To share ArchUnit rules across multiple repositories, authors must package them into a separate JAR (the official 'ArchRules' / Nebula Netflix pattern), publish it, and depend on it as a test-scope dependency.
ArchUnit has no built-in central-rule-server concept.

ArchUnit's ArchModule API (using @AppModule annotations on package-info) brings rule metadata back to colocation with the package being constrained — a deliberate move toward per-package denormalization for module-dependency declarations.
Netflix Nebula's ArchRules plugin exists because ArchUnit's built-in mechanism is per-repo by design.
ArchUnit is described as 'a popular OSS library used to enforce architectural code rules as part of a JUnit suite.'
claims.notes: Verbatim quote describing ArchUnit.

claims.text: Bazel's visibility attribute is declared per-target (denormalized), but Bazel's documented best practice is to factor repeated visibility lists into a package_group target that is referenced from multiple visibility attributes.
Bazel's package_group pattern is the hybrid pattern: declarations stay local while identifier bodies centralize when reuse warrants it.
Bazel docs instruct: 'Use package_group instead of repeating the list in each target's visibility attribute.'
claims.notes: Verbatim quote from official Bazel docs.

claims.text: Bazel also has a default_visibility package-level setter, which is a localized centralization (one BUILD file's targets share a default) — a third design point: per-package central with per-target override.

claims.notes: Migration case-study framing claim.

claims.notes: Shopify Packwerk original-design claim from the Rails at Scale retrospective.

claims.notes: Shopify Packwerk migration step 2.

claims.notes: Shopify Packwerk component-as-organizational-grouping reframing.

claims.text: Every surveyed system authors invariant declarations at the artifact they constrain (per-resource in Terraform; per-model in dbt; per-target in Bazel; per-test-class in ArchUnit; per-path-item in OpenAPI; per-subschema in JSON Schema).
claims.notes: Synthesis claim 1: authoring stays denormalized.

claims.text: None of the surveyed systems centralizes the declaration site for cross-file invariants.

Wherever the same invariant body or identifier list is reused, every surveyed system provides a centralization mechanism: components/schemas (OpenAPI), $defs (JSON Schema), package_group (Bazel), tests/generic/ macros (dbt), a separate ArchRules JAR (ArchUnit), or shared modules (Terraform).
claims.notes: Synthesis claim 2: bodies/identifiers centralize for reuse.

claims.text: Across the surveyed sources, centralization is for invariant bodies, not for declarations.
claims.notes: Load-bearing summary of the hybrid model.

claims.text: The trade-off vocabulary across surveyed sources is consistent: locality / churn / per-PV-discoverability (favoring denormalization) versus DRY / consistency / one-place-to-update (favoring centralization).
claims.notes: Load-bearing trade-off-vocabulary claim — design-frame language for the synthesis.

claims.text: When centralization makes change impact opaque, the named remedy across surveyed sources is automated breaking-change/impact-analysis on PRs, not retreat from centralization.
claims.notes: Load-bearing consensus-mitigation claim — cites Bump.sh, Redocly, and Shopify list-of-violations pattern.

claims.text: The Shopify Packwerk retrospective is the clearest 'adopted central, found it insufficient, walked back' datapoint among the surveyed systems.

claims.notes: Nuanced framing of the migration lesson.

claims.text: Hybrid (denormalized declaration, centralized body) is the documented sweet spot across every survey datapoint.
claims.notes: Load-bearing synthesis-conclusion claim.

claims.text: The surveyed sources favor a hybrid model — invariants declared at the artifact (denormalized) with reusable invariant bodies lifted into a centrally-referenced catalog.
claims.notes: Recommendation-framing claim from the research note.

claims.notes: Negative-evidence framing of the recommendation.
